title: Belong em Ação — M6: The São Teotónio Laundry

scenes.script_line: This is the module a lot of people will assume has nothing to do with them. It does. The São Teotónio laundry is the least visible unit at Craveiral and probably the easiest way to explain circular economy to anyone who doubts it. Because here there is no metaphor: a laundry set up to serve a hotel operation also serves the village it sits in. That is it. Circular economy in the plainest clothes there are.

scenes.script_line: It is worth seeing what the alternative would have been. A thirty-eight house hotel on the Costa Vicentina normally hands its linen to an industrial operator in a city, an hour or more away. Lorries covering that distance every week. Jobs created in another municipality. Nothing for São Teotónio. Building this here traded all of that for local employment, money circulating in this parish, and a service the village did not have and now does.

scenes.script_line: Now the part that matters to anyone in accommodation. Linen is the most intimate physical contact the guest has with Craveiral. Eight hours a night with their skin against our sheet. They touch our towel straight out of the shower, when they are most sensitive to everything. No amenity, no view, no dish makes up for a rough sheet or a towel that smells damp. This unit's work goes straight into the guest's sleep — and sleep is the most decisive wellbeing indicator of a stay.

scenes.script_line: The standard is measured in four things. Correct sorting on the way in: by type, by soiling, by temperature — most damage happens before the machine starts. Stain protocol on the first pass: a stain that goes through the dryer once never comes out. Traceability: we know which linen is from which house and which day, and what is out of circulation and why. And rejection without hesitation: a piece with a hole, a set stain or fraying never goes back on a bed. Cheaper to lose the piece than the guest.

scenes.script_line: Water and energy. A laundry is by nature the unit that consumes the most water and the most energy per square metre in the whole group. Which means it is also where a good decision is worth most. A full load instead of a half load. The right temperature, not the highest out of habit. Measured dosing, not by eye. Machine maintenance on a schedule, not on a breakdown. None of this is decorative ecology: it is the same waste-nothing logic we apply in the kitchen, applied where the numbers are bigger.

scenes.script_line: And the service to the village, which asks something not obvious. The neighbour who brings in a bag of washing is not a lesser customer because they do not sleep in one of our houses. Same treatment, same turnaround, same courtesy. On principle: we said we would open our doors to the village, and integration is judged by that, not by press releases. In practice: those people are our neighbours, some will be our colleagues, and all of them talk about us in the café. Local reputation is built one exchange at a time.

scenes.script_line: A word to the heads, because this unit carries a specific risk. It is physically demanding work, in heat, with little visibility and little spontaneous recognition — no guest writes a review praising the laundry. And our internal principle is explicit: we treat the team as we expect the team to treat the guest, and the standard is the same. In practice: breaks taken in August and not only in November, thermal conditions checked, and recognition said out loud when the work is good — because here nobody else will say it.

scenes.script_line: To close. A farm that preaches love of the land and runs a laundry wasting water is the same contradiction as a dead bulb on a boardwalk — except nobody sees it, which makes it easier to let happen. Coherence is the highest standard we have, and it is measured where nobody is looking. The short version: the back of house is the proof that the promise is true. In the last two modules we leave the units for what runs through all of them — experience and wellbeing.
